title: This Astronaut Has One Leg — and He Might Go to Space!
summary: Imagine floating in space, doing flips in the air, and looking down at Earth. Now imagine doing all that with one leg! That's what might happen to John McFall, a 45-year-old British surgeon and former Paralympic runner. When he was 19, a motorcycle accident led to his right leg being amputated (removed by doctors) above the knee. But he didn't let that stop him. He won medals as a sprinter, became a doctor, and in 2022 joined the European Space Agency's special program to see if a person with a disability could live and work in space. And guess what? He passed all the tests! Now, he's been chosen as a possible crew member for Haven-1, the world's first commercial space station, which could launch next year. John thinks his body might even have some advantages in space. Because he has less leg, less fluid might rush to his head in zero gravity — that's a problem that can blur astronauts' vision. Also, his bones might not weaken as much, which could lower the risk of painful kidney stones. But he says we won't know for sure until he actually goes up there and scientists run tests. "Is having two legs useful in space?" he wonders. We might soon find out!
why_it_matters: John McFall's story shows kids that having a disability does not mean you can't dream big and even reach for outer space.

background_read: The Paralympics are a major international sports event for athletes with disabilities, held right after the Olympics.
So far, every astronaut who has flown to space has had two functioning legs. John McFall could be the first person with a prosthetic leg to leave Earth.
Haven-1 would be the first space station built by a private company, not by a government space agency, opening space travel to more people.
Article_Structure: WHO: John McFall, a 45-year-old British surgeon and former Paralympic sprinter who has one leg.
WHAT: He has passed all tests and may become a crew member on the world's first commercial space station, Haven-1.
WHERE: He would launch from Earth to orbit in a spacecraft and stay on the new space station.
WHY: Because his body might have unexpected benefits in zero gravity, and scientists want to learn how disabilities affect living in space.

perspectives.description: Including a disabled astronaut sends a powerful message that space is for everyone, no matter how their body works.
Some people worry that a medical emergency with his prosthetic leg could be extra dangerous when far from Earth.
Studying his body in space might reveal new ways to protect all astronauts from bone loss and other health problems.
